editorial.summary: A contemporary KQED arts profile documents David Choe's Los Angeles graffiti argument, early San Jose reception, Double Rainbow and Five Color Cowboy work, fast mural process, late-2003 Tokyo incident and incarceration, religious uncertainty, and prison drawings made with improvised materials. The rolling-caption artifact is materially repaired by removing 244 measured 67-millisecond duplicate display states while retaining all 250 real caption units and every idea.

quality.assessment: Complete chronological human read. A deterministic rolling-caption normalization removes 244 duplicate display states and retains 250 real units / 1,324 words. Literal name/word damage is repaired; truncated opening, law, chronology, critical interpretation and speaker identity remain explicit.

editorial.speaker_policy: KQED captions mark speaker changes with >> but do not name the two arts commentators. Choe and narration are often distinguishable by content, but publication assigns zero line-level names until caption credits or held-out acoustic/video validation establishes them.

connections.relationship: Choe frames freeway graffiti as reaching more people than gallery display.
The early career story openly ties self-direction to unauthorized conduct.
KQED supplies contemporary, dateable claims about self-publishing, illustration and exhibitions.
Commentators place Choe inside an emerging cultural bridge rather than outside institutions entirely.
An ice-cream shop and hair salon function as early venues before conventional art-world acceptance.
The Five Color Cowboy commission joins Bay Area patronage to Choe's fast spray-paint process.
Witnesses value speed and low restraint, but their rhetoric does not prove absence of planning.
An art invitation becomes the setting for violence, arrest and a major creative/religious turn.
Choe attributes the encounter to misunderstanding; legal facts require independent records.
Isolation is central to the profile's explanation of religious reading and prison art.
The Bible becomes a resource in confinement while Choe resists a neat conversion narrative.
The first painting becomes a site of conflict between prior imagery and newly felt moral responsibility.
Choe's own word is searching, narrower than the commentators' found-God conclusion.
Drawings, writings and paintings become a distinct object corpus with unresolved publication format.
Soy sauce becomes pigment because conventional paint is unavailable.
A titled portrait links art object, injury, regret and the person Choe says he fought.
The critic celebrates reports from the edge; the archive preserves this without making harm a creative prerequisite.
The close reframes street art from irreverence alone toward meaning and substance.

editorial.description: A contemporary KQED arts profile documents David Choe's Los Angeles graffiti argument, early San Jose reception, Double Rainbow and Five Color Cowboy work, fast mural process, late-2003 Tokyo incident and incarceration, religious uncertainty, and prison drawings made with improvised materials.
